STATE OF NEW HAMPSHIRE 
PUBLIC UTILITIES COMMISSION 
 
DE 24-070 
PUBLIC SERVICE COMPANY OF NEW HAMPSHIRE d/b/a EVERSOURCE ENERGY 
Request for Change in Distribution Rates 
Order Communicating Affirmance of Order No. 28,170, With Certain Limited 
Modifications (As Requested by the Parties) 
 
O R D E R   N O.  28,201 
 
December 31, 2025 
 
 
On July 25, 2025, the Commission issued Order No. 28,170 establishing permanent 
distribution rates for Public Service Company of New Hampshire d/b/a “Eversource Energy” 
(“Eversource” or the “Company”), effective August 1, 2025, through July 31, 2029, under a 
multiyear rate plan adopted by the Commission. See Pub. Serv. Co. of N.H., d/b/a Eversource 
Energy, Order No. 28,170, (Jul. 25, 2025) at 69-70, 2025 N.H. PUC LEXIS 75, *98-*100. 
After rehearing, the Commission AFFIRMS IN PART, MODIFIES IN PART, VACATES IN 
PART, and CLARIFIES Order No. 28,170 consistent with this order.   
I. 
INTRODUCTION 
A. 
PARTIES AND INTERVENORS 
The Commission recognized the following parties to the rehearing on Order No. 
28,170: Eversource, the New Hampshire Department of Energy (DOE), the New Hampshire 
Office of the Consumer Advocate (OCA), and AARP New Hampshire (AARP) (collectively, 
the “Rehearing Parties”). See RSA 541:3 (2021) (allowing any party to the proceeding before 
the Commission, or any person directly affected thereby, to apply for a rehearing). After

granting each Rehearing Party’s motion for rehearing or clarification, no other person 
petitioned the Commission to intervene in the rehearing of Order No. 28,170. See RSA 541-
A:32, II (2021) (authorizing a presiding officer to grant petitions for intervention at any time 
in the interests of justice). 
B. 
PROCEDURAL HISTORY 
Included below is a summary of the procedural history in this case, with particular 
attention to the events occurring after July 25, 2025. 
On June 11, 2024, Eversource filed petitions seeking temporary and permanent 
distribution rate increases, with permanent rates to be based on a proposed 4-year 
performance-based ratemaking plan. On June 28, 2024, the Commission issued an order of 
notice commencing an adjudicatory proceeding, scheduling hearings to review the Company’s 
performance-based distribution rate proposal, and suspending the effective date of the 
Company’s proposed tariff. 
On July 19, 2024, Eversource, DOE, and OCA entered into a settlement agreement on 
temporary rates. See Eversource Energy Temporary Rates Settlement Agreement, Pub. Serv. 
Co. of N.H., Docket No. 24-070 (Jul. 19, 2024) [Tab No. 29]. In the settlement agreement 
filed with the Commission, Eversource, DOE, and OCA agreed, among other things, to allow 
Eversource to increase its fixed customer charge to $15.00, recover a $61,238,671 deficiency, 
and earn a 9.3 percent return on equity through temporary rates. Id. at 2, 5. According to the 
Company, DOE, and OCA, the temporary rates they agreed on increased the distribution 
portion of a Rate R residential customer’s bill by 14.64 percent, or a 5.27 percent increase to 
the total bill for an average Rate R residential customer. Id. at 2. On July 31, 2024, the 
Commission issued an order implementing the Company’s, DOE’s, and OCA’s agreed-upon

DE 24-070 
- 3 - 
 
temporary rates. See Pub. Serv. Co. of N.H., Order No. 27,041 (Jul. 31, 2024) (order approving 
temporary rates). The Commission observed in its order that the negotiated temporary rates 
in the settlement agreement were “. . . significant, which is concerning insofar as the scope of 
the increase could lead to ‘rate shock’ among Eversource's customers.” Id. at 5.     
On May 6, 2025, the Commission began 11 days of hearings on Eversource’s petition 
for permanent rates and its performance-based ratemaking plan. During and after those 
hearings, the Commission considered tens of thousands of pages of pre-filed and live exhibits 
and heard over 60 hours of witness testimony under cross-examination and subject to 
Commissioner questioning. At the conclusion of the hearings, the Commission held the record 
open to accept written closing arguments. The Rehearing Parties and certain other intervenors 
timely filed their written closing arguments with the Commission. 
On July 25, 2025, the Commission issued Order No. 28,170, establishing Eversource’s 
permanent electric distribution rates effective August 1, 2025, through July 31, 2029. See 
Order No. 28,170 at 69-70, 2025 N.H. PUC LEXIS 75 at *98-*100.  
Between August 1, 2025, and August 25, 2025, each of the Rehearing Parties filed a 
timely motion for rehearing or clarification of Order No. 28,170.   
On September 22, 2025, the Commission granted the Rehearing Parties’ motions for 
rehearing or clarification, and ordered the Rehearing Parties to provide further briefing to the 
Commission on the following questions: (1) “What if any cap should be placed on the New 
Start Program?” (2) “Was the Commission justified or not justified when adopting the 
escalating residential fixed customer charge?” and (3) “Whether the requirements of RSA 
378:28 for prudency reviews are applicable upon the adoption of multi-year rate plans 
pursuant to RSA 374:3-a and if applicable, how would this work for a multi-year rate plan?”

DE 24-070 
- 4 - 
 
On October 10, 2025, each of the Rehearing Parties filed a brief addressing each of 
the Commission’s questions. On October 24, 2025, each of the Rehearing Parties filed a sur-
reply brief further addressing the Commission’s questions. On October 30, 2025, DOE 
responded to the Company’s request, made in its sur-reply brief filed on October 24, 2025, 
for a stay of the so-called “New Start Cap.”  
Other than information for which confidential treatment has been requested of or 
granted by the Commission, Order No. 28,170, the motions for rehearing, and other docket 
filings are posted on the Commission’s website at: 
https://www.puc.nh.gov/VirtualFileRoom/Docket.aspx?DocketNumber=DE%2024-070. 
C. 
SUMMARY OF THE COMMISSION’S DECISION AFTER REHEARING 
After considering the respective pleadings of the Rehearing Parties and the underlying 
record in this contested case, the Commission is substantively divided on specific issues 
raised for rehearing or clarification, and on the final disposition of Order No. 28,170.  
Accordingly, for the reasons discussed below, Order No. 28,170 is AFFIRMED IN 
PART by a divided Commission, MODIFIED IN PART, as described below, to (1) initiate a 
prudency review of all Eversource’s capital expenditures made during calendar years 2025 
and 2026, VACATED IN PART as to the provisions of Order No. 28,170 that require or 
establish, or could be construed to require or establish: (2) any limitation on the rate recovery 
available to the Company for its New Start Program, including, without limitation, the 
provision in Order No. 28,170 requiring Eversource’s stockholders to absorb all costs of the 
New Start Program above the first $2.5 million recoverable through distribution rates; and (3) 
the $2.00 annual increase to the monthly Residential fixed customer charge, and CLARIFIED 
as to the provisions of Order No. 28,170 regarding (1) weather-normalization adjustments to

Eversource’s billing determinants; (2) the increase of the Residential fixed customer charge 
to $19.81 and corresponding reductions in volumetric rates; and (3) adoption of the DOE’s 
recommended 9.5 percent return on equity. 
II. 
POSITIONS OF THE REHEARING PARTIES 
A. 
EVERSOURCE’S POSITIONS 
Eversource filed at least two timely rehearing motions with the Commission, one on 
August 1, 2025, styled as a “motion for rehearing,” and another on August 25, 2025, styled 
as a “motion for clarification.” See Eversource Energy Motion for Rehearing and Limited 
Stay or Waiver in Part of Order No. 28,170, Pub. Serv. Co. of N.H., Docket No. 24-070 (Aug. 
1, 2025) [Tab No. 296] (the “Eversource Reh’g. Motion.”); Eversource Energy Motion for 
Clarification of Order No. 28,170, Pub. Serv. Co. of N.H., Docket No. 24-070 (N.H. P.U.C. 
Aug. 1, 2025) [Tab No. 303] (the “Eversource Clarif’n. Motion.”). 
1. Eversource’s Motion for Rehearing 
In its motion dated August 1, 2025, Eversource seeks rehearing on the Commission’s 
“decision requiring the Company to update [its] billing determinants and . . . associated 
weather-normalization routine on an annual basis, following the initial setting of rates 
effective August 1, 2025.” Eversource Reh’g Motion at 3. As grounds for rehearing, the 
Company asserts several related arguments to support its conclusion that the Commission’s 
rate formula, requiring Eversource to annually update to its billing determinants and 
associated weather-normalization routine, without its originally proposed K-bar determinant 
or other formulaic adjustment that provides reasonable revenue support through rates for its 
capital additions during the 4-year stay-out period, will not allow the Company to earn it its 
authorized rate of return, and, as a result, does not result in just and reasonable rates.

DE 24-070 
- 6 - 
 
a. Annual Updates to Bill Determinants and Weather-Normalization of Sales 
Firstly, the Company points out that while the requirement for the Company to 
annually update its billing determinants and weather-normalize its sales might mitigate rate 
effects on its customers, it will diminish the Company’s ability to earn its authorized return, 
by, among things, “stripping [away] any sales growth that has the potential to occur year-to-
year[.]” Id. at 3-4. The Company argues that without its originally proposed K-bar determinant 
“to support necessary capital investments” and “[w]ithout the ability to use sales growth to 
support capital additions, including most directly the capital additions enabling that sales 
growth, it will be [challenging] for the Company to maintain its financial integrity at a 
reasonable level across a [4]-year stay-out [period].” Id. at 4-5 (footnote omitted). 
Next, Eversource asserts that the Commission’s requirement for the Company to 
update its weather normalization routine and billing determinants annually, without an 
appropriate sales growth factor determinant, has resulted in the Commission adopting an 
alternative regulation framework that “does not methodologically align with either the 
Company’s proposal or the DOE’s suggested alternative” and, accordingly, is unsupported by 
record evidence. Id. at 6. The Company goes on to argue that “[i]n seeking to strike its own 
balance between customer and Company interests, the Commission has selected elements 
proposed by different intervenors to construct an alternative regulation framework that the 
Commission has deemed to be an appropriate balance between the interests of customers and 
the Company.” However, the Company further avers that “[b]y conceiving an alternative 
regulation formula that updates billing determinants without other interrelated adjustments, 
the Commission has inadvertently implemented a framework that will not be accurate or 
reasonable and is not supported by the record.”  Id. at 6-7.

DE 24-070 
- 7 - 
 
Thirdly, the Company argues that by “incorporat[ing] a weather normalization 
adjustment into the establishment of permanent rates, the Commission is seeking to mitigate 
rate impacts [on customers] . . . by controlling the revenues used in the calculation of rates.” 
Id. at 7. The Company disagrees with this approach because it could make it more difficult, 
if not impossible, for the Company to have a reasonable opportunity to earn its authorized 
return. Id. at 7-8. Furthermore, the Company believes that requiring it to weather-normalize 
its revenues may inappropriately penalize the Company, “despite the clear and 
[uncontradicted] record evidence that [electric] sales are not driven solely by weather and, in 
fact, sales have not correlated consistently with the magnitude of heating and cooling degree 
days.” Id. (citation omitted) 
Lastly, the Company cites other reasons why good cause exists for rehearing of Order 
No. 24,170, including, among others, the Commission’s choice of hypothetical capital 
structure for the Company, pointing out that it “is not aligned with the actual capital structure 
for the Company or any of its peer utilities (or the expectations of credit-rating agencies).” 
Id. at 9. 
b. Possible Remedies 
As possible remedies, the Company asserts that if the Commission sets aside the 
requirement in Order No. 24,170 for the Company to annually update its billing determinants 
and weather normalization routine, the Commission’s permanent rate framework “would 
produce similar revenues [for the Company] as a properly designed revenue cap formula (i.e., 
one that includes an explicit growth factor).” Id. at 9-10 (citation omitted). The Company 
suggests that “[a]n alternative approach would be to implement a growth factor as part of the 
Commission’s alternative regulation framework. However, the record does not contain

DE 24-070 
- 8 - 
 
evidence to support a particular growth factor[] and, accordingly, the Company does not 
suggest this remedy.” Id. at 10. 
2. Eversource’s Motion for Clarification 
In its Motion for Clarification dated August 25, 2025, the Company asks the 
Commission to clarify (a) the universal application of the weighted average cost of debt to 
deferred expenses; (b) the adjustments to rates following the audit of 2024 property taxes; 
and (c) certain procedural aspects of the annual alternative regulation rate adjustment filings.” 
Eversource Clarif’n. Motion at 1. 
a. Application of Weighted Average Cost of Debt to Deferred Expenses 
As to the “universal application of the weighted average cost of debt to deferred 
expenses[,]” the Company alleges “that the Commission found that, effective August 1, 2025, 
the carrying cost applied to all reconciliation and deferral accounts for the Company must be 
at the average cost of debt for the Company, calculated using the same weighting method as 
for computation of the weighted average cost of capital.” Id. at 3 (citation omitted). The 
Company goes on to state that “it is uncertain as to the basis of the Commission’s evidence 
or analysis regarding the Company’s ‘actual blended cost of debt’ and notes that the weighted 
average cost of capital established by the Commission in this proceeding is not based on the 
Company’s actual debt structure but rather a hypothetical structure.” Id. (footnote omitted). 
Although the Company claims, “it is not contesting the use [of] the average cost of debt, as 
specified by the Commission, for reconciliations and other annual carrying charges[,]” 
Eversource nevertheless points out that the Commission’s method does not reflect “the true 
cost” of carrying charges for the Company.” Id. Instead, the Company seeks clarification that 
the Commission did not intend to predetermine the appropriate carrying charges for deferred,

DE 24-070 
- 9 - 
 
but unrecovered, costs to be amortized over multiple years. Id. at 5. More specifically, the 
Company wants clarification as to whether “the unrecovered storm costs and such carrying 
charges will be addressed as part of the [ongoing] storm cost recovery proceedings in [Docket 
Nos.] DE 24-041 and DE 25-021.” Id. at 5-6. 
b. Treatment of 2024 Property Taxes 
As to the treatment of 2024 property taxes, the Company is concerned that although 
the Commission adopted the Company’s proposal to include property tax expense in base 
rates in Order No. 24,170, rather than annually through the regulatory rate adjustment (RRA) 
procedure, we also concurred with the DOE’s recommendation to defer the 2024 property tax 
recovery until after the DOE completes its audit of those taxes. Id. at 6. The Company asserts 
that although the Commission addressed the reconciliation of the 2024 property taxes 
following the conclusion of the DOE audit, Order No. 24,170 “does not expressly address 
how the adjustment to property taxes should be reflected in rates going forward.” Id. at 6-7. 
Accordingly, “the Company seeks clarification whether the Commission intends for the 
Company to propose a one-time adjustment to base rates as part of the alternative regulation 
framework or reconcile the difference between base rates and the audited 2024 property taxes 
annually until the Company’s next base distribution rate proceeding.” Id. at 7. 
c. Procedural aspects of the annual alternative regulation rate adjustment 
filings 
Regarding the annual alternative regulation framework reporting and adjustments, the 
Company seeks clarification from the Commission on potential conflicts between the 
Commission’s rules on annual filings and the reporting dates specified in Order No. 24,170. 
Id. at 7-8. Among other conflicts, the Company points to one requirement in Order No. 24,170,

DE 24-070 
- 10 - 
 
“that the Company must calculate inflation based on the quarterly GDP-PI published by the 
Bureau of Economic Analysis in April of the current year[,]” which conflicts with another 
requirement in Order No. 24,170 that mandates the Company supply its proposed rate 
adjustment, which is based on the inflation information that will not be published until April, 
in a March 1 filing. Id. at 8. As a remedy, the Company proposes to provide all available 
information to the Commission by March 1 of each year and to supplement its annual report 
by April 30 with the final quarter’s capital documentation. Id. at 10. 
B. 
DOE’S POSITIONS  
On August 22, 2025, the DOE filed its timely motion for rehearing of Order No. 
24,170, specifically seeking rehearing on, or clarification of, the Commission’s findings and 
rulings (1) to include the costs of the Company’s 2024 capital additions to plant in the $519 
million distribution revenue requirement effective August 1, 2025, (2) establishing the $519 
million “cast-off” distribution revenue requirement effective August 1, 2025, (3) establishing 
the alternative regulation framework, and (4) establishing the annual $2.00 increase to the 
fixed residential customer charge. See New Hampshire Department of Energy Motion for 
Rehearing on Order No. 28,170 Establishing Permanent Rates and Alternative Regulation 
Through July 31, 2029, Pub. Serv. Co. of N.H., Docket No. 24-070 (N.H. P.U.C. Aug. 22, 
2025) [Tab No. 300] (the “DOE Reh’g Motion”). 
1. Inclusion of the 2024 Capital Additions to Plant in the $519 Million 
Distribution Revenue Requirement 
The DOE asserts that “the Commission may have overlooked or mistakenly conceived 
the requirements of RSA 378:28 when reaching its decision, resulting in an order that is both 
unlawful and unreasonable.” DOE Reh’g Motion at 8. The DOE argues that the permanent

DE 24-070 
- 11 - 
 
distribution rates the Commission set in Order No. 24,170 are unjust and unreasonable 
because they are based on the $519 million distribution revenue requirement effective August 
1, 2025, that includes both the costs and a return on the costs of the Company’s 2024 capital 
additions to plant, in violation of the prohibition contained in RSA 378:28 (2009) against the 
Commission including “in permanent rates any return on any plant, equipment, or capital 
improvement which has not first been found by the commission to be prudent, used, and 
useful.” Id. 
As a remedy, the DOE requests that the Commission’s order after rehearing set new 
permanent distribution rates after finding a different distribution revenue requirement 
effective as of August 1, 2025, that, at a minimum, excludes all costs and any return on costs 
associated with the Company’s 2024 plant additions. The DOE also requests that the 
Commission’s order after rehearing, “only allow recovery in rates of the [costs of the 
Company’s 2024 plant additions] once [the Commission] has found these plant additions to 
be prudent, used, and useful.” Id. at 9. 
2. Establishment of the $519 Million Distribution Revenue Requirement 
The DOE requests rehearing of, or clarification regarding, how the Commission 
arrived at the $519 million “cast-off” distribution revenue requirement effective August 1, 
2025. DOE Reh’g Motion at 10.  
a. The Order’s $519 Million Determination Lacks the Required Findings and 
Underlying Facts required under RSA 541‑A. 
The DOE contends that Order No. 24,170 does not specify how the Commission 
calculated the $39,417,837 increase to the distribution revenue requirement. DOE Reh’g 
Motion at 11. While the DOE concedes that Order No. 28,170 identifies certain inputs, e.g.,

DE 24-070 
- 12 - 
 
cost of capital, ROE, and disallowances, it does not show the math. See id. Without an 
itemized derivation, including how each determination affected revenue requirement line 
items, Order No. 28,170 cannot satisfy the statutory requirement for findings of fact supported 
by explicit underlying facts. DOE Reh’g Motion at 11-12. Nor does the Order disclose 
whether the Commission relies on staff or consultant analysis not otherwise in evidence. Id. 
at 12. If the Commission did rely on such materials, they must be noticed and are contestable. 
Id.  
b. The Order Is Internally Inconsistent Regarding the “First Implementation” 
of Alternative Regulation 
The DOE further argues that Order No. 28,170 states the alternative regulation formula 
begins August 1, 2026, yet it claims the $519 million “includes… the first implementation of 
the alternative regulation annual rate increase.” DOE Reh’g Motion at 11.  Absent a clear 
explanation of what “first implementation” means for 2025, e.g., whether an I‑X‑like 
increment is embedded or whether certain escalations were treated as transitional cast‑off, the 
Order is ambiguous and may be unlawful. Id. at 11-12. The DOE goes on to point out that if 
alternative regulation does not begin until 2026, then any 2025 increment attributed to that 
framework must be disclosed and justified. Id. at 12. 
As a remedy, the DOE requests that the Commission clarify whether any alternative 
regulation increment is embedded in the 2025 cast‑off figure, and if so, itemize it and justify 
its inclusion before 2026 implementation.  
c. Recoupment Under RSA 378:29 Cannot Be Computed Without a 
Segregated, Itemized Breakdown 
The DOE contends that neither it nor the Company can lawfully compute recoupment 
unless the Commission segregates the permanent revenue requirement tied to the 2023 test

DE 24-070 
- 13 - 
 
year from any alternative regulation‑related increments, including, for example, the 2024–
2025 cast‑off additions. The DOE points out that while Order No. 28,170 acknowledges that 
recoupment pertains to the permanent rate 2023 test‑year revenue requirement and not to the 
post‑2023 folding‑in of alternative regulation increments, because the $519 million cast-off 
blends these elements, the correct recoupment cannot be derived. 
Additionally, the DOE maintains that any 2024 capital expenditure costs must first be 
found prudent, used, and useful before they are included in rates; consequently, such costs 
must also be excluded from recoupment unless and until those findings are made. 
As a remedy, the DOE requests that the Commission provide an explicit recoupment 
schedule that (i) extracts all non‑permanent/alternative‑regulation increments from the $519 
million cast-off, (ii) excludes unadjudicated 2024 capital items, and (iii) yields a computable 
difference between temporary and final permanent rates for the temporary‑rate period. 
d. The Order No 28,170 Risks Carrying Forward Temporary‑Rate 
Assumptions That Are No Longer Applicable 
The DOE asserts that the $61,238,671 temporary rate increase included one‑time 
normalizations, such as the CCI Pole Purchase, and relied on the capital structure approved 
in the Company’s rate case in Docket No. DE 19‑057, not the capital structure ultimately 
approved in Order No. 28,170. Any derivation of the $519 million that carries forward these 
temporary assumptions would be arbitrary and contrary to the record. The permanent revenue 
requirement must rest on a uniform set of assumptions—specifically, the final capital structure 
and the removal of non‑recurring items—to avoid contaminating the cast‑off base that will be 
subject to future I‑X adjustments.

DE 24-070 
- 14 - 
 
As remedies, the DOE requests that the Commission clarify whether the 
temporary‑rate assumptions are included in the calculation of permanent rates. If the 
temporary‑rate assumptions are included, the DOE requests that the Commission remove them 
from the permanent rate calculation. The DOE also requests that the Commission certify that 
non‑recurring items and superseded capital structures have not been carried forward into the 
$519 million cast-off revenue requirement. 
e. Applying I‑X to O&M at 2023 Levels May Create Annual Increases 
Exceeding the Commission’s 1% O&M Cap 
The DOE next avers that if the cast‑off base includes O&M at 2023 test‑year levels, 
and that base is subject to I‑X annually, revenues tied to O&M may increase beyond 1% per 
year, even when the Company holds spending within the cap to avoid prudency review. That 
mismatch risks creating unintended incentives and outcomes (i.e., increased revenues without 
proportionate O&M growth), undermining the cap’s purpose. 
As remedies, the DOE asks the Commission to clarify whether O&M dollars within 
the cast‑off base are inside the I‑X mechanism; if so, re‑scope or exclude O&M or adopt a 
countervailing adjustment so that I‑X does not produce revenue growth in excess of the 1% 
O&M cap absent demonstrable need and adjudicated prudence. 
f. The $2.5 Million New Start Budget Should Be Excluded from I‑X and 
Clearly Segregated 
DOE states that Order No. 28,170 approves a $2.5 million annual New Start budget 
and that the Company’s shareholders must bear the costs above the cap. Although the record 
reflects the Company’s willingness to exclude certain components from annual inflation 
adjustments, and the DOE requests clarification from the Commission that the New Start 
program is outside the I‑X base. The DOE argues that including New Start within I‑X would

DE 24-070 
- 15 - 
 
automatically increase the program’s funding, contrary to the Commission’s express budget 
cap and cost‑containment design.  
As a remedy, the DOE asks the Commission to confirm that the $2.5 million New Start 
budget is excluded from the I‑X calculation and is tracked separately with no inflation uplift, 
consistent with the Order’s budgeted approach and shareholder overrun responsibility. 
3. Alternative Regulation Framework Generally 
The DOE seeks rehearing and clarification of the Commission’s alternative regulation 
framework. DOE Reh’g Motion at 16. In its motion, the DOE argues that (a) the Order No. 
24,170 overlooks material record evidence and lacks findings showing just and reasonable 
Rates for Eversource’s New Hampshire customers. Id.; (b) the negative X‑Factor functions as 
a de facto K‑Bar, pre‑funding capital before prudency and “used and useful” findings, in 
violation of RSA 378:28 (2009). DOE Reh’g Motion at 20; (c) Order No. 28,170 fails to make 
the required public‑interest findings under N.H. Admin. R., Puc 206.06(b) and Puc 206.07(c). 
DOE Reh’g Motion at 21; and (d) the Commission’s annual spending threshold of $250 
million improperly substitutes a spending cap for prudency review and lacks an appropriate 
claw-back mechanism. Id. 
a. Order No. 28,170 Overlooks Material Record Evidence and Lacks Findings 
Showing Just and Reasonable Rates for Eversource’s New Hampshire 
Customers 
The DOE asserts that the expert testimony of its witness, Mr. Dudley, established that, 
in general, (i) Performance-Based Rate plans are untested in New Hampshire, (ii) that the 
results of Eversource’s Performance-Based Rate plan in its Massachusetts service territory 
should be observed first, and (iii) that the Company’s capital planning history shows 
aggressive and sometimes poorly managed investments. The record also shows that

DE 24-070 
- 16 - 
 
COVID‑related cost escalations are waning, yet the Commission nevertheless encourages up 
to $250 million in annual spending—well above the Company’s historical norms, even 
including pandemic‑impacted years. The DOE argues that Order No. 28,170 does not address 
these concerns nor articulate findings demonstrating why a novel ratemaking regime will 
result in just and reasonable rates. The DOE points out that N.H. Admin. R., Puc 206.06(b) 
requires the Commission to make findings on New Hampshire‑specific considerations before 
approving alternative regulation, particularly on reliability, regulatory balance, administrative 
efficiency, economic development, universal service, innovation, infrastructure, and 
environmental safeguards. The absence of explicit findings on these factors and of any 
analysis connecting the framework to just and reasonable rates constitutes reversible error 
and warrants rehearing. 
As remedies, the DOE requests that, after rehearing, the Commission make findings 
of fact and rulings law as to (x) why novel alternative regulation is appropriate now for New 
Hampshire; (y) how the Commission’s alternative regulation framework ensures just and 
reasonable rates in light of the Company’s historical capital spending; and (z) how the 
Commission’s alternative regulation framework addresses the specific factors in N.H. Admin. 
R., Puc 206.06(b). 
b. The Negative X-Factor Functions as a De Facto K-Bar, Pre-Funding 
Capital before Prudency and “Used and Useful” Findings, in Violation of 
RSA 378:28 (2009) 
The DOE alleges that the Commission merely replaced the Company’s proposed K‑Bar 
with a negative X‑Factor and annual inflation increases for capital and overhead. Still, the 
mechanism’s label does not alter the economic reality: if the framework provides revenue 
support for ongoing capital investments before prudency review, then it pre‑recovers costs in

DE 24-070 
- 17 - 
 
contravention of RSA 378:28 (2009). The Commission’s prudency review trigger at $250 
million per year is no substitute for project‑level prudency determinations, and the absence 
of a rate claw-back feature exposes Eversource’s customers to the risk of irreversible 
pre‑funding of imprudent spending. The DOE points out that the Commission recognized that 
prudency findings should not be short‑circuited by alternative regulation. Order No. 28,170 
at 48. Yet, under the Commission’s alternative regulation framework, capital spending below 
the cap may flow through rates without contemporaneous prudency determinations. 
As remedies, the DOE requests that the Commission clarify whether its alternative 
regulation framework pre‑funds capital prior to prudency and “used and useful” 
determinations. If yes, the DOE requests modifications to (x) eliminate pre‑recovery, (y) 
require contemporaneous prudency review, and (z) implement a rate claw-back mechanism 
for any amounts later found imprudent or not used and useful. 
c. The Order Fails to Make Required Public‑Interest Findings under N.H. 
Admin., R Puc 206.06(b) and Puc 206.07(c) 
The DOE asserts that N.H. Admin. R., Puc 206.07(c) mandates that alternative 
regulation may be approved only if it “serves the public interest,” after considering and 
making findings on the nine factors in N.H. Admin. R., Puc 206.06(b). Although Order No. 
28,170 alludes to rate smoothing, earnings predictability, and administrative efficiency, see 
Order No. 28,170 at 4, 48–49, it does not expressly analyze and balance the nine enumerated 
factors. Missing are findings on (i) how the framework affects competition; (ii) safety, 
adequacy, and reliability; (iii) the traditional regulatory balance among customers, investors, 
and stakeholders; (iv) administrative efficiency vs. due process in prudency review; (v) 
economic development implications of accelerated capital outlays; (vi) universal service; (vii)

DE 24-070 
- 18 - 
 
innovation; (viii) infrastructure improvements with measurable outcomes; and (ix) 
environmental/conservation safeguards. Without these required findings, the Commission’s 
order implementing alternative regulation does not satisfy the requirements of N.H. Admin. 
R., Puc 206.07(c), and is therefore unlawful and unreasonable. 
As remedies, the DOE suggests that the Commission, after rehearing, either make 
specific findings under N.H. Admin. R., Puc 206.06(b) and Puc 206.07(c), or, in the 
alternative, remand Order No. 28,170 to the Commission for supplemental findings and record 
development.  
d. The Commission’s Annual Spending Threshold of $250 Million Improperly 
Substitutes a Spending Cap for Prudency Review and Lacks an Appropriate 
Claw-back Mechanism 
The DOE asserts that the Commission’s prudency review trigger, based on whether the

RSA 362:2, I (Supp. 2024). Consequently, Eversource must “file with the public utilities 
commission, and shall print and keep open to public inspection, schedules showing the rates, 
fares, charges and prices for any service rendered or to be rendered in accordance with the 
rules adopted by the [C]ommission pursuant to RSA 541-A[.]” RSA 378:1 (2009). Unless the 
Commission otherwise orders, no change shall be made in any rate, fare, charge, or price, 
which shall have been filed or published by a public utility, here, Eversource, in compliance 
with the requirements hereof, except after 30 days’ notice to the Commission and such notice 
to the public as the Commission shall direct. RSA 378:3 (2009).  
Whenever a public utility files any schedule with the Commission stating new and 
higher rates, fares, charges, or prices, which the public utility proposes to put into force, the 
Commission may investigate the reasonableness of such proposed rates, fares, charges, or 
prices. RSA 378:5 (2009). Pending any investigation of a rate schedule which represents a 
general increase in rates and the decision thereon, the Commission may suspend the taking 
effect of said schedule and forbid the demanding or collecting of the rates, fares, charges, or 
prices covered by the schedule for such period or periods, not to exceed 12 months in all, as

(2009).  
The Commission is authorized to fix rates after a hearing, upon determining that the 
public utility’s proposed rates, fares, and charges are “just and reasonable.” RSA 378:7 (Supp. 
2024). New Hampshire recognizes at least two “just and reasonable” standards applicable to 
public utility ratemaking: (a) a statutory “just and reasonable” standard based on traditional 
ratemaking methods. See, e.g., RSA 378:27-:28 (2009 & Supp. 2024) (rates must be at least 
“sufficient to yield not less than a reasonable return on the cost of the property of the utility 
used and useful in the public service less accrued depreciation.”); and (b) a broader 
constitutional standard under which “[a] just and reasonable rate is one that, after 
consideration of the relevant competing interests, falls within the zone of reasonableness 
between confiscation of utility property or investment interests and ratepayer exploitation.” 
In re Pub. Serv. Co., 130 N.H. 265, 274 (1988).  
In determining whether rates are “just and reasonable,” the Commission must balance 
customers’ interest in paying no more than required with investors’ interest in obtaining a 
reasonable return on their investment. Appeal of Eastman Sewer Co., 138 N.H. 221, 225 
(1994) (citation omitted). In this way, the Commission serves as the arbiter between 
customers’ interests and those of the regulated utilities. See RSA 363:17-a (2009); see also 
Appeal of Pinetree Power, 152 N.H. at 100. 
The statutory standards for the sufficiency of ratemaking decisions do not require the 
Commission to “determine [an] outcome using any specific methodology, so long as the result 
is consistent with the ‘public interest’ and the rates are ‘just and reasonable.’” Northern

MOTIONS FOR REHEARING 
RSA chapter 541 governs our procedure for rehearing, except as otherwise provided 
by law. RSA 365:21 (Supp. 2024); Appeal of Office of Consumer Advoc., 148 N.H. 134, 135-
36 (2002). RSA 541:3 (2009) provides, “[w]ithin 30 days after any order or decision has been 
made by the commission, any party to the action . . ., may apply for a rehearing . . ., specifying 
in the motion all grounds for rehearing, and the commission may grant such rehearing if in its 
opinion good reason for the rehearing is stated in the motion.” RSA 541:3 (2009). “Such 
motion shall set forth fully every ground upon which it is claimed that the decision or order 
complained of is unlawful or unreasonable.” RSA 541:4 (2021); Appeal of Camp’gn. for 
Ratepayers Rights, 145 N.H. 671, 674 (2001) (citing Appeal of Richards, 134 N.H. 148, 154 
(1991)). A successful motion for rehearing does not merely reassert prior arguments and 
request a different outcome. See Abenaki Water Company, Inc., Order No. 26,312 at 8-9 
(2019).  
A movant can establish a “good reason" for rehearing in one of three ways: firstly, the 
movant establishes that there were matters we “overlooked or mistakenly conceived in [our] 
original decision.” Dumais v. State Pers. Comm'n, 118 N.H. 309, 311 (1978); secondly, the 
movant establishes that new evidence is available that could not have been presented at the 
original hearing. See Appeal of Gas Serv., Inc., 121 N.H. 797, 801 (1981); O’Loughlin v. N.H. 
Personnel Comm’n, 117 N.H. 999, 1004 (1977); or thirdly, the movant demonstrates that our 
order is unlawful or unreasonable by other means. RSA 541:4 (2021); see, e.g., Amsler v. S.

Hampton, 117 N.H. 504, 506 (1977) (citation omitted) (holding that an order is subject to 
remand if the basis for the board’s decision cannot be determined from the order).  
“Notwithstanding RSA 541:5, upon the filing of a motion for rehearing, the 
commission shall within 30 days either grant or deny the motion, or suspend the order or 
decision complained of pending further consideration, and any order of suspension may be 
upon such terms and conditions as the commission may prescribe.” RSA 365:21 (Supp. 2024). 
If the Commission grants a motion for rehearing, we may hold another hearing or reconsider 
the matter and either reissue our original order or issue an amended one. See 5 GORDEN J. 
MACDONALD, NEW HAMPSHIRE PRACTICE: WIEBUSCH ON NEW HAMPSHIRE CIVIL PRACTICE 
AND PROCEDURE § 62.33 (3d ed. 2010). The Commission’s statutory power to reconsider and 
modify an existing order is limited only in that the modification must satisfy the requirements 
of due process and be legally correct. Appeal of Office of Consumer Advoc., 134 N.H. 651, 
658 (1991) (citing Meserve v. State, 119 N.H. 149, 152 (1979)); see also RSA 365:28 (2009).
